title: Inventory, managed settings and spend ceilings
bridge: The agent inventory is like the dependencies list in package.json: one reviewed file that says what each agent may pull in. Except npm installs whatever you list. Here the broker and the gateway enforce the list later, so a wrong line becomes a wrong permission.
intro: This lesson writes three data files in RhinoHealth/ai-agents: the agent inventory, the managed settings and the spend limits. No code runs here, but the broker, the gateway, the orchestrator and Security all read these files later. Get them right now, and the later goals have one answer to 'what may this agent do'.

picture.caption: Three reviewed files, and the places that read them.

steps.text: writes one row per agent: model, data, keys, repos, channels
opens a PR; Security reviews this one and every later change
writes deniedModels: fable and agent teams off, nothing else
pasted into server-managed settings, so every laptop gets it
writes far-away limits with mode: shadow
reads hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90; new runs wait, running ones finish

p: Open RhinoHealth/ai-agents and look at three paths: inventory/agents.yaml, settings/managed-settings.d/10-models.json and settings/spend-limits.yaml. None of them is code. Each one is data that other parts of the platform read, and each one answers one question.

agents.yaml answers 'what may this agent touch'. 10-models.json answers 'which models and features are off for everyone'. spend-limits.yaml answers 'how much may people and agents spend, and what happens near the limit'.
All three change only through a PR. For the inventory, Security (Ronen) reviews the PR. That is the point: Security reviews one file instead of five systems.

callout.text: The broker (G3), the gateway and the routine charters (G5) all need one answer to 'what may this agent touch'. The inventory is that answer.

sections.h: The inventory: Byte and Vanil, live today
p: An inventory is a list of every AI agent. Each row says what it does, its model and vendor, and the data it sees. It also names its keys, its owner, and the exact repos, tools and Slack channels it may use. We start with the two agents that run today, Byte and Vanil.

Byte's row comes from its real config: the model and effort from byte src/engines.ts, the repos from config/repositories.json. Vanil's row comes from its n8n credentials, so you fill it with Nave. Where a value is not confirmed, the file says so in a comment instead of guessing.

Byte has two vendors. Anthropic serves the review model. TypeSafe is an outside company, and Jev is its model. Byte uses Jev for the sniff: a cheap check, on each new push, of whether Byte's open findings were fixed (lesson g2-3).
sections.because: We write the live agents first because their access already exists, so the file must match reality before it describes anything planned.

code.text:
# ai-agents/inventory/agents.yaml
# Every AI agent and exactly what it may touch. Changes are PRs reviewed by Security (Ronen).
- name: byte
  status: live
  owner: nave
  does: advisory PR reviews, sniff, fix mode
  model: claude-opus-5-5, effort high              # byte src/engines.ts
  vendors: [anthropic, typesafe]
  data: diffs and comments of PRs in installed repos; no PHI
  keys: [BYTE_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, BYTE_CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, BYTE_TYPESAFE_API_KEY]   # org Actions secrets
  github: { app: byte-review, repos: installation roster, writes: [COMMENT reviews, fix PRs into the author's branch] }
  slack: ["#byte"]
  unattended: true
- name: vanil
  status: live
  owner: nave
  does: Vanta to Jira compliance sync, policy renewal redlines
  model: claude-opus-5                             # confirm with Nave
  runs_on: n8n.example.com (inf)
  data: Vanta tests, RH Jira tickets, policy docs in Google Drive; no PHI
  keys: n8n credentials (list them with Nave)
  slack: ["#vanil", "#security", "#grc-committee"]
  unattended: true

notes.text: The rule in one line: every later change to an agent's access is a PR, and Security reviews it.
One list item per agent. The name is the key other files use: the gateway workload, the ZDR workspace.
'does' is plain words. Byte posts advisory reviews, runs the sniff, and can open fix PRs.
The model and effort are copied from src/engines.ts, not guessed; the comment says where to look.
Two vendors: Anthropic for the review model, TypeSafe for the Jev sniff.
What data the agent sees. 'no PHI' is a wall, and every row must say it.
Byte's keys are org Actions secrets. The names let you find them; no value is ever written here.
The GitHub App, which repos (its installation roster) and the only writes it may do.
unattended: true means nobody approves each run; Byte reviews on its own.
Vanil's model is not confirmed, so the comment says 'confirm with Nave' rather than guessing.
Vanil's keys live in n8n's credential store; list their names with Nave.
Three Slack channels: the exact set Vanil posts to today.

sections.h: The inventory: Nova, the planned agent
p: For a planned agent you write the narrowest set that works. That means one repo, the token permissions the broker grants, one Jira issue, one Slack thread. Routines that run unattended get no Jira writes beyond their own ticket. The broker scopes in G3 and the routine charters in G5 are built from these rows.
After Nova, add rows for the routines, the brain bot and the eval runner in the same shape. Then open the PR and ask Ronen to review it.
sections.because: We write Nova's row now because the broker and the gateway are built to grant exactly this and nothing more.

code.text:
- name: nova
  status: planned (G3, G4)
  owner: sean
  model: routing table, Opus 5.5 at medium by default
  vendors: [anthropic (ZDR org, workspace nova)]
  data: fcp code and fake seed data only
  keys: none in the VM; the broker holds GitHub, Jira and Slack; the gateway holds Anthropic
  github: { app: rhino-ai-agents, repos: [fcp], token: "contents and pull_requests write, 1 h, one repo" }
  jira: the assigned issue only
  slack: the ticket's thread only
  unattended: false                                # one person approves the plan, a different one the PR

notes.text: The same list continues. Nova is our ticket-to-PR agent.
status says which goals build it, so a reader knows this row is a plan, not a fact yet.
The model comes from a routing table (lesson p8-8): Opus 5.5 at medium effort unless a step says otherwise.
The Anthropic key lives in the ZDR org, in a workspace named nova (lesson g0-2). A workspace is one billing and key boundary inside the org.
The wall in one line: no keys in the VM. The broker holds GitHub, Jira and Slack; the gateway holds Anthropic.
One GitHub App, one repo, a 1-hour token with contents and pull_requests write only.
Jira access is the assigned issue, nothing else.
Slack access is the ticket's thread, nothing else.
unattended: false. One person approves the plan and a different person approves the PR, never the requester.

p: Managed settings are Claude Code settings an organisation sets for every user, and a person cannot override them (lesson p12-2). We ship one small file: it blocks the Fable models and keeps agent teams off. Nothing else changes, so people keep Anthropic's model and effort defaults.

Why block Fable? Fable needs 30-day data retention, a compliance call we have not made, and it is not available under ZDR. Agent teams are an experimental feature that lets several sessions work as one team; the ticket keeps it off. Do not set availableModels, model or effortLevel: subagents and workflows keep using the session's model.

The file reaches people and agents by two different roads. People: paste it into claude.ai Admin Settings, under Claude Code managed settings (server-managed). Agents: G3's Packer image copies it to /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d/. Sessions that sign in with a Console API key do not receive server-managed settings.
sections.because: We keep the source in git so each change to the rules is a reviewed PR, not a console click.

notes.text: $schema lets your editor check key names against Claude Code's settings schema.
deniedModels hides a model family everywhere. It needs Claude Code v2.1.283 or later.
env sets environment variables for every session, the way a .env file would.
CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=0 keeps agent teams off.

sections.see:
On a laptop after the rollout, inside claude:
/status  lists the managed settings source
/model   shows Fable hidden or greyed out
sections.ifInstead: If /model still offers Fable, check the Claude Code version: deniedModels needs v2.1.283 or later.

sections.h: Spend: see it before you limit it
p: The rule for spend is: look first, limit later. No limit may cut a run in the middle. So every ceiling is far away, starts in shadow mode, and is set from 4 weeks of real data. Shadow mode means the limit only logs what it would have done.

People first. Each person sees their own spend with /usage and the status line, and nobody sees a per-person list. In the Claude admin console, set alerts on the R&D pool at 50, 75 and 95 percent. The R&D pool is the shared Enterprise budget all of R&D draws from.

No per-person caps during W3 to W7. On 18 Nov (W7), book 30 minutes with Ronen. The extra-usage limit per person is set at about 3 times a heavy user's real month; the first guess is about $500. The first 'request more' each month is approved automatically.
Agents next. In the ZDR org, give each workspace (nova, routines, brain-bot) a monthly limit of about 3 times its expected spend. Set alerts at 50, 75 and 90 percent, sent to #ai-agents-alerts.

The numbers go into one file, so the orchestrator and the G1 spend view read the same values. The one setting that acts is hold_new_runs_above_pct. Above 90 percent of a workspace limit, new runs wait in the queue while running ones finish. A run that already started is never cut.
sections.because: We put the limits in a file, in shadow mode, so each one is watched for 4 weeks before it acts.

code.text:
# ai-agents/settings/spend-limits.yaml
# Far-away limits only. Each one logs what it would have done for 4 weeks (shadow) before it can act.
# No limit stops a run in the middle: limits act before a run starts or between turns.
mode: shadow
people:
  observe_until: 2026-11-18            # end of W7: no new caps before this
  extra_usage_limit_usd: null          # set in W7 at ~3x a heavy user's real month (first guess ~500)
  first_request_more_each_month: auto_approve
  later_requests: a lead approves the same day
  rnd_pool_alerts_pct: [50, 75, 95]    # Enterprise R&D pool
  visibility: own spend only (/usage, status line); team totals in Grafana, never names
agents:                                # one ZDR workspace and one gateway workload each
  nova:      { monthly_limit_usd: null, alerts_pct: [50, 75, 90], hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90 }
  routines:  { monthly_limit_usd: null, alerts_pct: [50, 75, 90], hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90 }
  brain-bot: { monthly_limit_usd: null, alerts_pct: [50, 75, 90], hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90 }
  # monthly_limit_usd: about 3x expected spend, filled in when the workspace limit is set
burn_rate_alert:                       # built in G1 (spend view)
  ahead_of_budget_pct: 25
  notify: [sean, nir]

notes.text: Every limit logs for 4 weeks before it may act. That is what shadow means.
The wall: limits act before a run starts or between turns, never in the middle.
mode: shadow is the switch the orchestrator reads. Nothing acts while it says shadow.
No new caps for people before 18 Nov, the end of W7.
null on purpose: the number is set in W7 from real data, at about 3 times a heavy user's month.
The first 'request more' each month is approved automatically; later ones a lead approves the same day.
The three alert points on the Enterprise R&D pool.
Visibility is own spend only. Grafana shows team totals and never names.
One row per agent workspace. monthly_limit_usd is filled in when the workspace limit is set, at about 3 times expected spend.
hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90 is the hold: above 90 percent, new runs wait in the queue; running ones finish.
The burn-rate alert is built in G1: it fires when the month runs 25 percent ahead of budget.
Sean and Nir get that alert.

callout.text: No time, turn or budget limit cuts a run. A hold applies to runs that have not started; it never stops one that has.

sections.h: The lab's test: parse and assert
p: The lab checks the three files the way the orchestrator will: parse them and assert the shape. The yaml package parses YAML, and JSON.parse reads the settings file. node:test (lesson p1-6) holds the assertions. This file is the lab's test, not a platform file.
sections.because: We test data files because a typo in a key name is silent in YAML and loud in a test.

notes.text: parse from the yaml package turns YAML text into plain objects and arrays.
Only the fields the test reads. Everything else in a row is allowed and ignored.
Top-level await works because package.json says "type": "module".
The first test looks only at rows whose status starts with 'planned'.
'keys' in a checks the key exists, even when its value is a sentence like 'none in the VM'.
mode must be the word shadow, so a typo like 'shadows' fails.
Every agent block must hold new runs at 90; the comment line in the YAML is not a key.
deepEqual compares the whole array, so ["fable", "opus"] would fail.

quiz.q: The brain bot needs one more Slack channel. What do you do?

options.text: Ask Nave to add the channel in n8n and tell the broker team
options.why: n8n is Vanil's home, not the brain bot's, and a chat message is not a reviewed change.

options.text: Open a PR to inventory/agents.yaml and ask Security to review it
options.why: The inventory is the one place access is written; every change is a PR reviewed by Security.

options.text: Change the broker's scope config and open the inventory PR later
options.why: The broker is built from the inventory, so the file changes first, then the scope follows.

quiz.q: Why does G3's Packer image copy 10-models.json to /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d/?

options.text: Because agents need a different model list from people
options.why: The file is the same for both; only the road it travels differs.

options.text: Because the admin console only reaches laptops on VPN
options.why: VPN has nothing to do with it; server-managed settings reach laptops anywhere.

options.text: Because sessions that sign in with a Console API key do not receive server-managed settings
options.why: Agents sign in with a key through the gateway, so the file must be on the VM's disk.

quiz.q: Nova's workspace reaches 92 percent of its monthly limit while three runs are working. What happens?

options.text: The three runs finish; new runs wait in the queue until spend is under 90 percent
options.why: hold_new_runs_above_pct acts before a run starts, never on a run in progress.

options.text: The gateway returns 429 and the three runs stop at the next call
options.why: The gateway reports spend and never refuses a call over budget.

options.text: Each run is cut at its next turn to save the remaining 8 percent
options.why: No time, turn or budget limit cuts a run in the middle; that is a wall.
